hero.narrative_lead: The machine spent everything to erase his name from the ballot. It cannot erase
hero.narrative_run: Byron Sigcho-Lopez is running for a third term as Alderman of the 25th Ward. The campaign launched August 18, 2026 in Pilsen, blocks from where the congressional run was announced.
hero.summary: On July 21, 2026 the electoral board voted unanimously to strike his name from the November ballot, 1,222 signatures short after their lawyers finished. Byron is challenging Illinois's signature rules in federal court, in his words, so our community never again has to accept an appointed candidate. And he is home in the ward that built the movement, where on February 23 the neighbors answer.

promise.label: The Promise Kept
promise.headline: They Said It Couldn't Be Done.
promise.beat1: Illinois law demanded 10,816 valid signatures from an independent. The machine's candidate needed 697.
promise.beat2: At the announcement, a reporter asked if it was even possible. The room raised its hands before Byron could answer.
promise.cite: Shouted from the room at the announcement
promise.close: They did not beat this at the doors. Their lawyers challenged signatures until the count fell 1,222 short of 10,816, and the rule that let them do it is now being challenged in federal court. On February 23, 2027, the 25th Ward votes, and objections do not count. Voters do.

bio.label: Meet Byron
bio.headline: Byron Sigcho-Lopez is a father of triplets and the independent socialist alderman who closed a 23 year chapter of machine corruption in the 25th Ward.
bio.p1: Byron is an immigrant who came to the United States alone when he was 17 years old. His life is a testament to what happens when strangers become neighbors and family.
bio.p2: Since 2019 he has delivered for the ward, not for donors. Over 800 units of affordable housing created or preserved. The largest vacant site in Pilsen, at 18th and Peoria, won for at least 280 affordable units instead of luxury development. Over $500,000 in state funds for violence prevention. Over $1 million in infrastructure for Benito Juarez Community Academy. Ward Night every Tuesday, including through the pandemic.
bio.p3: He is running for a third term because the work is not finished. Rent stabilization and a property tax system that protects seniors and working families. An elected school board. A reopened Department of the Environment. A Discount Mall that stays. A ward office that answers to neighbors and not to developers.
bio.p4: Byron earned his Bachelor's in Mathematics and Business Administration from Cumberland University and his Master's in Economics from the University of Illinois at Chicago. He lives in Pilsen with his wife, Loreen, their triplets, a dog, and two cats.
bio.quote_card: "It takes people and people defeats money."

platform.label: The Record
platform.headline: What the 25th Ward built, and what we finish next.

housing.title: 800 units of affordable housing, and 18th and Peoria won
housing.desc: Over 800 units of affordable housing created or preserved since 2019. Byron won public investment for the largest vacant site in Pilsen, at 18th and Peoria, for at least 280 affordable units instead of luxury housing that would have accelerated displacement. He passed protections for homeowners and seniors against predatory developers, and opened zoning decisions to a resident Zoning Advisory Board.

safety.title: Safety built block by block
safety.desc: When City Hall left violence prevention out of the budget, Byron worked with state and county partners to bring over $500,000 for public safety infrastructure to the ward and $80,000 for programming at Rudy Lozano Alternative High School. Neighbors organized 2532 to reduce gun violence block by block, and the ward office works street by street with residents on the root causes of harm.

schools.title: Strong schools, open libraries, air you can breathe
schools.desc: Over $1 million in state infrastructure for Benito Juarez Community Academy and other 25th Ward schools, and the process started to expand the Rudy Lozano library. Byron joined the hunger strike to #StopGeneralIron, won a commitment to a cumulative burden health impact study, held MAT Asphalt accountable in McKinley Park, and got environmental justice into city procurement.

accountability.title: Not for sale, and never was
accountability.desc: Byron took disgraced former Alderman Danny Solis all the way to the Illinois Supreme Court and won changes to campaign finance rules so indicted politicians cannot spend campaign funds on their legal defense. He does not take contributions from large corporations or developers, and he has upheld that commitment every year in office.

anointment.label: Round One
anointment.headline: The Anointment
anointment.step1: Rep. Chuy García filed for a fifth term, telling no one he planned to retire.
anointment.step2: Moments before the deadline, his former chief of staff filed petitions collected in just days. He withdrew and endorsed her. She needed only 697 signatures.
anointment.step3: On March 17, IL-04 voters got exactly one choice. Independents had to collect over 10,816 signatures for November.
anointment.step4: 22,788 of your neighbors answered. So on June 9, the machine sent lawyers to throw your signatures out.
anointment.step5: On July 21, 2026, the electoral board voted unanimously to strike Byron from the November ballot, 1,222 signatures short of 10,816 after their lawyers finished. Fellow independent Mayra Macías was struck by the same three objectors. The seat was handed over without a competitive election.
anointment.step6: Byron took Illinois to federal court over a rule that demanded 10,816 signatures of him and 697 of the machine's candidate. He is honest that reinstatement is unlikely. He filed anyway, so our community never again has to accept an appointed candidate.
anointment.kicker: They needed lawyers to win round one. Round two is in federal court. Round three is the 25th Ward, on February 23, 2027, where no one can object to your ballot.

meet.hero_badge: INDEPENDENT DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST • CHICAGO DSA • 25TH WARD
meet.hero_sub: From Ecuador to Tennessee to Pilsen. Byron Sigcho-Lopez came to this country alone at 17 and has spent his life fighting alongside the working class as a teacher, researcher, organizer, and unapologetic democratic socialist.
meet.hero_thesis: "Justice is not a destination. It is the road that is traveled." This is the road that made Byron.
meet.origin_p1: Byron first came to the United States alone as a teenager, settling in Tennessee and then moving to the Chicago area and Pilsen over 10 years ago. He was born and raised in Quito, Ecuador and came to the US following political instability in the country, and a tragic car accident that left his mother in a coma.
meet.origin_p2: Emergency services were nearly non-existent during this period, and his family's lives were saved by passing motorists who stopped, rescued his family from the wreckage, and drove them to the hospital. When his mother awoke from the coma, she insisted her eldest leave the country for his last year of high school.
meet.origin_p3: When Byron arrived in Tennessee at the age of 17, he knew no one in the country and did not speak English. He was taken in by a generous family who gave him a home and helped him pursue an education.
meet.education_p1: Byron first visited Chicago with his Tennessee family who had loved ones in the Chicago area. During this first trip, they brought Byron to Pilsen to have dinner at the Nuevo Leon restaurant.
meet.education_p2: After graduating high school in Tennessee, Byron was able to attend college on a soccer scholarship after receiving an honorable mention for the All-State Tennessee Soccer Team in high school. Byron graduated from Cumberland University with his Bachelors in Mathematics and Business Administration.
meet.education_p3: He was also awarded the prestigious President's Award for his exceptional academic performance, and many contributions and successes in the school community during his time there. After graduation, Byron returned to Chicago and eventually settled in Pilsen to start his life.
meet.record_desc: Byron became an adult education teacher at the University of Illinois at Chicago and founded the UIC Center for Literacy's Spanish literacy program, making the GED program at UIC much more widely accessible to Spanish speaking immigrants and residents. Seeing the need for wrap-around services, Byron also brought a case worker into the program to ensure his students' families received resources and needed services.
meet.record_desc2: In addition to Byron's work as a teacher, he also volunteered as a youth soccer coach at Pilsen Academy. Byron earned a Master's Degree in Economics from UIC while also working as a lead researcher. He began collaborating alongside the Chicago Teachers Union in investigating the financial relationships between charter school networks like UNO, school funding, and Chicago's political elite, and organized with parents and teachers like Karen Lewis to fight for fully funded public schools.
meet.schools_desc: After Rahm Emanuel announced that he would be closing a hundred thirty Chicago Public Schools, Byron became involved in the Pilsen Alliance where he organized with the community to push to keep the schools open.
meet.first_run_desc: In 2015, Byron was encouraged by community leaders Nellie Cotton and Kit Duffy to run for Alderman against the machine - now disgraced former Alderman Danny Solis. Byron came in second in the 5-way race.
meet.alliance_desc: Byron eventually served as the Director of Pilsen Alliance where he became a leader and an activist in the fight against gentrification, displacement, and corruption.
meet.dsa_desc: He joined forces with organizers from the Chicago Democratic Socialists of America while partnering on the coalition to Lift the Ban on Rent Control across the state of Illinois, and became a member then and there.
meet.elected_headline: A Grassroots Movement, Not a Machine Candidacy
meet.elected_p1: In 2019, Byron ran a grassroots campaign for Alderman of the 25th Ward. He committed to refuse political contributions from developers and big corporations - a commitment he has upheld to this day and beyond. Since taking office, any resident now can personally meet with Byron at his weekly Ward Night, and all residents can receive compassion, support, and city services from the devoted public servants who staff the 25th Ward office.
meet.elected_p2: In 2023, big money and the political establishment lined up against Byron. Byron took democratic establishment and corrupt Danny Solis all the way to the Illinois Supreme Court over his unethical campaign finance practices. The voters of the 25th Ward sent him back to City Hall.
meet.elected_2026: In 2026, the movement he built gathered 22,788 signatures to put Byron on the congressional ballot as an independent, more than double the 10,816 the law demanded of him and far more than the 697 the machine's own candidate needed. On July 21, 2026, the State Officers Electoral Board voted unanimously to strike his name from the ballot, ruling him 1,222 signatures short.
meet.elected_2026b: Byron did not stop there. In late July 2026, he filed a federal lawsuit against the Illinois State Board of Elections, arguing that the state's signature requirements for independents are unconstitutional. In his words: "so our community never again has to accept an appointed candidate." Then he came home to run for a third term representing the 25th Ward.
meet.elected_p3: As an elected official, he used the power of his office to put the people's power into the institutions that needed it - under his leadership, change is happening.
meet.achieve_housing_desc: Byron has preserved and created over 800 units of affordable housing across Chicago and as Chairman of the Committee on Housing and Real Estate, made Chicago the largest city to pass a $135 million dollar investment via the Green Social Housing Initiative, to build sustainable housing and help address the housing crisis in Illinois.
meet.achieve_wardnight_desc: Every community member has the opportunity to speak directly with their elected official every Tuesday at the Ward Office - the accountability is a commitment.
meet.achieve_health_desc: The Pilsen Food Pantry has grown to serve more than ever. Perpetrators of heinous crimes are held accountable more often and public safety has become more possible for the community to organize for. A dental clinic accessible to the people was opened and a mental health clinic as well.
meet.achieve_fight_desc: Property tax payers know that their elected official has voted against every single proposed property tax increase, and worked to fight for a statewide millionaire surcharge and wealth taxes on the billionaires. When Trump sent ICE to our communities, Byron faced them head on with the full weight of his office and his community ensuring that Bovino and other thugs were held accountable to the furthest extent possible in court.
meet.elected_call: Byron has changed what was possible in public service on the municipal level and he isn't stopping. We need him back at City Hall for the 25th Ward.
meet.family_desc: Byron, and his wife Loreen, live in Pilsen with their little triplets (who attend public school), and their dog, Buster, and their two cats Dos and 三歲.

meet.caption_schools: Fighting for investment in our neighborhood schools

issues.hero_headline: Not Promises. Receipts. Seven Years Delivering for the 25th Ward.
issues.hero_sub: In 2019, Byron Sigcho-Lopez took the 25th Ward from a 23-year machine and never took a dime from it. This is what he delivered as your Alderman, and what he is fighting for next.
issues.another_world: Another world is not only possible. It is necessary.
issues.another_world_sub: In the 25th Ward, we are already building it.
issues.public_safety_title: Public safety, built block by block
issues.public_safety_desc: When City Hall left violence prevention out of the budget, Byron went around it. He brought more than $500,000 in state funding for public safety infrastructure into the ward, plus $80,000 for programming at Rudy Lozano Alternative High School.
issues.public_safety_desc2: Out of his regular community safety meetings, neighbors built 2532, a resident-led organization that applies block-by-block strategies to reduce gun violence and address its root causes across the 25th Ward.
issues.public_safety_desc3: He has pushed the Chicago Police Department for accountability on low clearance rates, worked with victims of violence and their families to get answers, and backed residents and business owners raising concerns on their own blocks.
issues.housing_caption: Listening to neighbors, door to door
issues.housing_title: 800 units delivered. Rent stabilization is next.
issues.housing_desc: Byron has supported the development and preservation of more than 800 units of affordable housing in the 25th Ward since 2019. He fought for public investment to buy the largest vacant site in Pilsen, at 18th and Peoria, to build at least 280 units of affordable housing there instead of the luxury development that would have accelerated displacement.
issues.housing_desc2: He co-chaired the mayor's Affordable Requirements Ordinance task force and helped double the ARO minimum from 10% to 20%, passed legislation protecting homeowners, seniors, and longtime residents from harassment by predatory developers, and built a Zoning Advisory Board that puts neighbors from every part of the ward into zoning decisions.
issues.housing_desc3: Now he is fighting for rent stabilization and to reform the property tax system so seniors and working families are not taxed out of the neighborhoods they built.
issues.schools_title: Every school funded, every library open
issues.schools_desc: As a teacher himself, Byron knows what our schools and libraries mean to the strength of this community. He worked with the State of Illinois to secure more than $1 million in infrastructure improvements at Benito Juarez Community Academy and other 25th Ward public schools, and he initiated the long-overdue expansion of the Rudy Lozano Public Library.
issues.schools_desc2: He stood against retaliation targeting teachers, including a 25th Ward resident, after they joined the fight against environmental racism during the General Iron hunger strike. He is fighting for fully funded public schools and an elected school board now.
issues.environment_caption: Raising his voice for environmental justice
issues.environment_desc: Byron joined the hunger strike to stop General Iron from relocating its pollution into a working-class community already overburdened with toxic industry, and he has demanded accountability for the disastrous Hilco implosion. He won a commitment to a cumulative burden health impact study, now underway, and he is at the table writing legislation to stop the concentration of toxic polluters in our neighborhoods.
issues.environment_desc2: He has held MAT Asphalt accountable for polluting McKinley Park and led the effort to add environmental justice criteria to city procurement contracts. Now he is fighting to reopen the Department of the Environment so climate and environmental justice concerns are handled by the city, not left to chance.
issues.gender_equity_title: Reproductive justice and a ward office that leads
issues.gender_equity_desc: Byron pushed the Mayor's Office, alongside his colleagues, to increase funding for LGBTQIA+ inclusive social and health services, and supported legislation making Chicago a reproductive health sanctuary city.
issues.gender_equity_desc2: He is proud to lead the first 25th Ward office with a majority-female leadership team, including his Chief of Staff.
issues.constituent_services_title: Every Tuesday night, the doors are open
issues.constituent_services_desc: Every Tuesday, including through the pandemic, Byron hosts Ward Night so residents and stakeholders can bring their concerns directly to him. During the pandemic, he and his team personally delivered masks, sanitizer, and safety supplies across the ward, and his office built an emergency fund of nearly $100,000 for residents who did not qualify for other assistance, including undocumented neighbors.
issues.constituent_services_desc2: His team pushes 311 to fill potholes and fix streetlights, led the repaving of Cermak Road, and every winter his office and volunteers shovel for elderly and disabled residents and organize neighborhood cleanups each spring and summer.
issues.economic_caption: On the picket line with striking workers
issues.economic_title: Standing with workers and small businesses
issues.economic_desc: Byron supported the creation of the Pilsen Chamber of Commerce so small businesses have direct, self-determined access to resources and advocacy, and he is working to integrate the Pilsen and Little Village chambers so the whole ward benefits. When an Amazon distribution facility in the ward failed workers on bathroom access and air conditioning, his office moved fast to win changes.
issues.economic_desc2: He walked the line with unionized and organizing workers across the city, stood with the small businesses of the Discount Mall to keep them on 26th Street, helped the Pilsen Food Pantry move into a larger space where it now feeds more than 1,500 neighbors a month, and fought to get small businesses reimbursed for license fees they paid but couldn't use during the COVID shutdowns.
issues.transparency_title: He took Solis to the Supreme Court and won
issues.transparency_desc: Byron took disgraced former Alderman Danny Solis all the way to the Illinois Supreme Court and won changes to campaign finance rules so indicted politicians can't spend campaign funds on their own legal defense. He has strengthened the Office of Inspector General as it exposed the Hilco implosion, the illegal raid on Anjanette Young, and public safety failures in our communities.
issues.transparency_desc2: Byron has never taken a dime of corporate or developer money since 2015, and he never will. He is fighting for publicly financed elections, a LaSalle Street tax on the more than a quadrillion dollars in financial transactions that pass through the Chicago Mercantile Exchange tax-free every year, and a public bank so our small businesses and residents can access credit on fair terms.
issues.transparency_desc3: In 2026, when that same political establishment used the courts to strike his name from the congressional ballot, Byron didn't stop fighting. He took Illinois's ballot-access laws to federal court, in his words, so our community never again has to accept an appointed candidate.
issues.unbought_text: Byron completely rejects corporate PAC money and contributions from large real estate developers, a commitment he has kept since 2015. He only answers to the working-class coalition of the 25th Ward. His campaign is funded by small-dollar donations from neighbors, teachers, union members, and working families. This is what it means to be truly independent.
issues.unbought_press_quote: "Lopez has admirably represented his ward in his first term... Lopez is endorsed."
issues.unbought_kicker: "It takes people and people defeats money."

machine.hero_sub: In July 2026 they showed exactly what they will do to democracy: strike a name from the November ballot rather than face the voters. You cannot disqualify a neighborhood. The movement took the fight to federal court and came home to the 25th Ward, where voters, not objectors, decide on February 23, 2027.
machine.movement_intro: Byron Sigcho-Lopez is an ideologically committed democratic socialist and a firebrand who has spent his entire career fighting for the multiracial working class. He is not a politician looking for a promotion. He is an organizer who was called to serve by his community.
machine.unbought_text: Unlike establishment politicians, Byron completely rejects corporate PAC money and contributions from real estate developers. His campaign is powered entirely by thousands of small-dollar grassroots donations from teachers, nurses, union members, and working families. He has upheld this commitment since his first campaign in 2015 and has never wavered.
machine.tested_text: Byron's unique power comes from bottom-up organizing. As 25th Ward Alderperson, he passed anti-displacement legislation to protect homeowners from predatory developers, created over 800 units of affordable housing, stood uncompromisingly with the Chicago Teachers Union, doubled the Affordable Requirements Ordinance minimum, and joined a hunger strike to fight environmental racism. These are not campaign promises. These are receipts.
machine.pullquote: "I have never taken a dollar from a corporation or a developer. I never will. My loyalty is to the people of this district, not to the machine."
machine.thesis: "Democracy cannot be preserved nationally if it is subverted locally."
machine.timeline_intro: What happened in IL-04 is not an isolated incident. It is part of a broader, dangerous pattern of the establishment insulating itself from the working class.
machine.timeline_2016: The DNC weaponized the undemocratic superdelegate system to block progressive momentum and override the will of grassroots voters.
machine.timeline_2020: The party establishment swiftly coalesced in a coordinated effort to block Bernie Sanders' grassroots movement, consolidating behind a single candidate overnight.
machine.timeline_2024: The party suppressed primary challenges and skipped debates, culminating in a late Biden drop-out and an uncompetitive process that left voters demoralized and demobilized.
machine.timeline_now: In IL-04, the same playbook ran at the local level. A Congressional seat was handed to a handpicked successor, 22,788 voters answered anyway, and in July 2026 an electoral board struck the independent from the ballot instead of letting voters decide.
machine.cta_headline: They Erased a Name. They Cannot Erase a Neighborhood.

volunteer.hero_headline: We Know How to Knock On Doors. Now We Do It for the Ward.
volunteer.hero_sub: We don't have corporate PAC money or backroom bosses. We have you. Join the multiracial working-class coalition that keeps the 25th Ward unbought and re-elects Byron Sigcho-Lopez.
volunteer.hero_status: THE WARD CAMPAIGN BEGINS. ELECTION DAY: FEBRUARY 23, 2027.
volunteer.blitz_alert: JULY 21, 2026: THE BOARD SIDED WITH THE MACHINE
volunteer.blitz_headline: They Erased the Name. Not the Movement.
volunteer.blitz_p1: You did it. The law demanded 10,816 valid signatures from an independent, while the machine's candidate needed just 697. This movement collected and filed 22,788, more than double the requirement. That was never in question.
volunteer.blitz_p2: On July 21, 2026, the State Officers Electoral Board voted unanimously to strike Byron from the November ballot, ruling he came up 1,222 signatures short of the 10,816 bar after the machine's lawyers finished challenging them. Round one went to their lawyers. But you cannot disqualify a neighborhood, and the movement that gathered 22,788 signatures came home to the ward that built it. The fight didn't end there either: in late July 2026, Byron sued the Illinois State Board of Elections in federal court over the signature burden itself. His words: "so our community never again has to accept an appointed candidate." Round two happens at the ballot box, February 23, 2027, where objections don't count and voters do.
volunteer.blitz_promise: The room promised 20,000. You delivered 22,788. Round two is February 23, 2027.
volunteer.picker_sub: Don't turn on each other. Uplift each other. Help each other. Show solidarity. Pick what sounds like you and we'll point you to your post.
volunteer.picker_hint: Pick one or more. We'll check the boxes for you below.
volunteer.canvass_desc: Knock on doors in Pilsen, Little Village, McKinley Park, and the rest of the 25th Ward to have meaningful, one-on-one conversations about housing, economic justice, and keeping this ward unbought. This is how movements are built: at the doorstep.
volunteer.events_desc: Every Tuesday is Ward Night: neighbors bring their questions straight to Byron's team. Help staff Ward Night, table at block parties and community events, and put a face to this campaign at the places where the ward already gathers.
volunteer.digital_desc: Reach voters where they are through rapid-response text campaigns, phone calls, and social media. This work can be done from anywhere, anytime, and is critical for expanding the movement beyond what door-knocking alone can achieve.
volunteer.precinct_desc: Lead the ground game in your neighborhood. Precinct captains coordinate local volunteers, organize neighbors to re-elect Byron on February 23, 2027, and serve as the backbone of the campaign at the block level. Not selected? Support your captain however you can.
volunteer.creative_desc: Design flyers, create campaign videos, and push content across social media. From graphic design to videography and video editing, your creative skills can amplify Byron's message to thousands of voters.
volunteer.campus_desc: High school ambassadors and college campus captains help mobilize the next generation. Organize voter registration drives, host campus events, and build a youth coalition that fights for affordable education and a livable future.
volunteer.signup_desc: Fill out the form and our team will reach out with next steps. Whether you have one hour or one hundred, there is a role for you in this movement.

duel.r1_machine_text: Chuy Garcia filed for a fifth term, waited until the final hours before the deadline, then handed the seat to his former chief of staff. She needed 697 signatures. Voters got one choice.
duel.r1_movement_text: We did not wait for the Democratic Party to give us permission. Byron announced in Pilsen at Cinco Estrellas, blocks from the classrooms where he taught.
duel.r1_movement_quote: "I do not build coalitions with politicians. I build coalition with my constituents."
duel.r2_machine_text: They publicly celebrated how secret the operation was, then introduced their candidate by playing in our faces about silencing our voices for another cycle.
duel.r2_movement_text: A reporter asked if an independent could even collect 10,816 valid signatures. The room answered before Byron could.
duel.r3_machine_text: Illinois election law demanded 10,816 valid signatures from an independent. Their candidate needed 697.
duel.r4_machine_text: This cycle in Illinois, $20 million from AIPAC, big tech oligarchs, and corporate interests denied people across the state the chance for fair elections.
duel.r4_movement_text: Byron asked for 1,000 grassroots donations to put that campaign in full swing. The movement answered with more. Average gift: $27. No corporate PACs, no lobbyists, no AIPAC. Ever. That has not changed.
duel.r4_movement_quote: "It takes people and people defeats money."
duel.r5_machine_text: Machine lawyers combed every line, challenging every misspelled name and every address one digit off, working to erase 22,788 voices one signature at a time, in a process built to drag through the summer.
duel.r5_movement_text: The movement defended every line. Neighbors, volunteers, and essential workers sat through the hearings for signatures they had gathered themselves, asking for one thing: let the people decide.
duel.r6_machine_text: In July 2026 the State Officers Electoral Board voted unanimously to strike Byron from the November ballot. After their lawyers finished with the petitions, the count came up 1,222 short of 10,816. The board chair told the candidates they had "just come up short." Independent Mayra Macias was struck the same day by the same three objectors, and the path was clear for their candidate.
duel.r6_movement_text: Byron sued the Illinois State Board of Elections in federal court. The suit argues that demanding 10,816 signatures from an independent while asking 697 of a party candidate unconstitutionally restricts voters under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. His attorneys told him reinstatement was unlikely. He filed anyway.
duel.r6_movement_text2: Then the movement came home. Byron is running for re-election as Alderman of the 25th Ward, the ward the machine lost in 2019 and has never taken back. Round one went to their lawyers. Round two is February 23, 2027, where objections do not count and voters do.
duel.r6_movement_quote: "This is being done so our community never again has to accept an appointed candidate."

timeline.s4_desc: A machine-backed objector files a challenge to throw out your signatures and erase your choice.
timeline.s5_desc: Records exams and hearings at the State Board of Elections. The movement defends every line while machine lawyers work to strike them.
timeline.s6_desc: The State Officers Electoral Board votes unanimously to strike Byron from the November ballot, 1,222 short of 10,816 once the challenges are done. Independent Mayra Macias is struck the same day by the same three objectors.
timeline.s7_desc: Byron sues the Illinois State Board of Elections, arguing that 10,816 signatures for an independent against 697 for a party candidate unconstitutionally restricts voters under the First and Fourteenth Amendments. Reinstatement is unlikely. He filed anyway, for everyone who comes next.
timeline.s8_desc: August 18: the movement packed Indígó MRKTŌ in Pilsen to launch the re-election campaign. The congressional run started in Pilsen too. Byron runs for a third term as Alderman of the 25th Ward, the ward the machine lost in 2019 and has never taken back.
timeline.s9_desc: Not the machine. Not their lawyers. No objection can strike a ballot. You decide.

counter.readout_label: valid signatures filed with the Illinois State Board of Elections. The record stands.
counter.marker_law: What the law demanded of Byron
counter.caption: Promise made. Promise kept. Then erased by lawyers, never by voters.

voices.label: From the Announcement
voices.headline: The People Vouch
voices.victoria_quote: Boogie lives within Byron. We need him to take us to a grander scale.
voices.mariam_quote: A real leader shows up when you need them the most.
voices.robert_quote: A guy helping you that does not know you at all says something about the person. Trust the heart.
voices.jesse_quote: He will look out for you. He will not sell you out. His door is always open.
voices.farah_quote: He does not just talk the talk. He embodies the struggle of his community and the promise of what it can be.
voices.lee_quote: People before party. It will always be like that, and he is the man.
voices.cta: Add your voice. Help re-elect Byron on February 23, 2027.

road.quote: Justice is not a destination. It is the road that is traveled.
road.lead: Round one went to their lawyers. Round two is the ballot box, February 23, 2027.

ticker.p4: So our community never again has to accept an appointed candidate.
